Famously, Rylance turned down a role in Spielberg's Empire of the Sun to remain with the RSC.

Later, Spielberg called Pete "the best actor in the world". After he died, Spielberg put Rylance in the Bridge of Spies role that would have likely been Pete's... and Rylance won an Oscar for that.

So I think Mark Rylance carries on his legacy. When people have praised Rylance's acting style in interviews, he just cites Pete as the pioneer. Dude really idolized him like an older brother.

Anyway, watch The Outfit (2022)

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. The Odyssey being rated R is proof the MPAA is due for serious reformation

**Score:** 270
**Body:** The movie is absent of nudity, gore, and has no F-bombs. 



We see arrows go through armed baddies but no close-up shots of arrows penetrating skin. They’re very little blood oozing out.



Penetration with sharp objects itself should be PG-13. To get an R, consider if the aftermath of the wound is shown, if there’s visible blood during penetration and the amount, if it’s a close-up shot vs. wide shot, and how much time spent on the shot. 



If the same battle used Star Wars lightsabers and blaster rifles instead of metal arrows, it’s PG-13. But because of the technicality that arrows exist and they’re sharp, an orange considered. The weapon choice is an absolutely an insane determinate.



Likewise, if the one-eyed monster were eating aliens who bleed green goo or androids who ooze sparks instead of red sanguine like we have, it’s PG-13. 



There’re no long shots of humans being graphically eaten. They’re very brief shots of bites, quickly edited, very little blood if any, with the action being far away in the shot concealed in the shadows. 



Telemachus slits the throat of a baddie, but we only hear the sound effect and see the sword on his neck, but we do not see the laceration being made or the aftermath. 



We get an implied beheading. The statue symbolism is what a filmmaker would show when they want to you to know what happens without actually showing it. Innuendos exist for that purpose. 



If Nolan knew he was making an R, he could have gone harder in that flashback scene by showing real dismemberment and lacerations - because it would have been an R anyway. All visible evidence point to the sign that Nolan was at least trying to make a PG-13 film when filming this, by how many times the film actually held back by NOT showing you the thing, but at the end of the day, said “Screw it, I’m a brand” rather than shave 20 seconds off the movie for resubmission. 



It’s frankly pathetic that this an R. The MPAA should be the most lenient with content in film as compared to Northern European countries, but instead the American system is closer to Sharia Law. 



The content shown here is what I’d expect and desire from a dark PG-13 comic book film. This is a family friendly movie; it’s on the very dark side of a family friendly movie, but it’s a family friendly movie a family of two parents and two tweens can enjoy. If this gets the same rating as Last House on the Left, America has a serious rating problem. America needs to desensitises itself to what it considers mature content. 

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I’m surprised you took the time to write this post but missed that there are indeed a few “fucks” in the film. I let out a laugh when Odysseus said “10 years on this fucking beach. Time to go home” or something to that effect.  

To finalize, I’d like to share the Freakazoid! bit with Jack Valenti where he explains the rating system: 
https://youtu.be/SzbE0wpqeKc?si=ViuM_NBg5yeEVE_r
  - Frankly, I also wonder how much the 'animal transformation' affect anything.

It isn't graphic or anything - but it is a fairly disturbing scene, especially for a 13 year old.

Does something that isn't graphic, yet disturbing, count for anything in the rating?
    - I also wonder if the cyclops eating men skews close enough to cannibalism which is one of those taboo topics that might upset the MPA.
2. Nolan himself said he knew it would likely be rated R and it was included in his original negotiations with Universal. He's pretty familiar with the MPA guidelines at this point.

I do agree that the MPA could do with some changes, and it's silly to put Odyssey in the same category as a hardcore slasher or anything really graphic. But Odyssey was made with an R rating in mind, at least according to Nolan.
  - It's funny that even knowing that, Nolan doesn't lean into making use of that R-rating at all.
    - it's probably more to do with the fact that he didn't want to feel creatively restricted by a pg-13 rating, even if he wasn't planning on make the odyssey super explicit anyway
    - Given his sensibilities, I don’t think he’s gonna throw up gore just because he can. I think the movie was as violent as he wanted it to be
3. I agree in the abstract since The Odyssey is fairly tame and shouldn't have the same rating as far more adult films, and more importantly that the MPAA needs to be reformed. But I think singling out The Odyssey isn't an optimal example. 

The problem with the MPAA has traditionally been caring little about violence and focusing on sexuality. I had one teacher who hyperbolized by saying 'if a man cuts off a breast it's pg-13 but if he kisses a breast it's R' but there's a truth to that. And The Odyssey is quite sexless considering the source material has him fucking godesses left and right.

The Odyssey was rated R because they dropped a few F bombs. It seemed Nolan was deliberate about that choice and he wanted it to be R, maybe after realizing with Oppenheimer that his stock was so high he could make a rated-R film without limiting his audience.

I can't imagine him holding back on violence because he thought he could make it pg-13, he just doesn't like visual depictions of violence. 

IMO Odysseus really should have been drenched in blood in that final slaughtering, Homer compared him to a lion after a slaughter, but that's not Nolan's vibe.
4. Mild gore and three f-bombs. I don't think it deserves an R rating, but these are the reasons.

The absolute worst offender is The King Speech being R rated when it should probably be PG. 
5. I find the American eating system very odd. There's a really big stigma around a movie being NC-17 and so most adult films are R. Here in the UK and "adult" movie would be a 15 or an 18, and there's no stigma about either rating.

For example in America, The Matrix and Aliens are both rated R, but in the UK they're 15 and 18 respectively.

The Matrix is a fun action romp, it's got a tiny bit of body horror, but overall it's dudes shooting other dudes.

Aliens is visceral and scary. It's got chest bursters, it's got people dying covered in weird goo on walls, it's distressing imagery, its gorey.

In my mind it makes sense that these movies got 2 different ratings, I'd show a 10 year old The Matrix, but probably not Aliens.

## 2. Resurrection (2025) - Bi Gan

**Score:** 27
**Body:** I was trying to watch this movie since its release in Cannes and, as the saying goes, "When there's a will, there's a way". I finally made it, and it totally surpassed my wildest expectations.

I'm in awe. Conceptual, innovative, visually stunning, complex, with multi-layered narratives and three subjects very close to me: cinema, Chinese history and Buddhism. And an ode to art — and cinema — as a form of exploration in a society that worships technology and pure rationality.

Again, as a Buddhist, this is the second time I've come across an audiovisual project structured around this belief while simultaneously exploring other, similar narratives or related themes. Coincidentally, or perhaps not, both were Chinese productions released in 2025. Regarding the other two topics, many have already mentioned the story of cinema; while they also represent Chinese history in the 20th century.

It's impossible to write something in detail; the post would be endless, and I still need to process everything. Simply marvellous!

To watch and rewatch many times, for whatever reason you choose. ...if you like/are familiar with at least one of them mentioned in the second paragraph.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. It’s truly great. I still think it’s the best I’ve seen this year by a mile. I was lucky to have a local theatre also show Long Days Journey into Night which I would heavily recommend if you enjoyed Resurrection.  
  - I haven't watched it, but I think Long Day's Journey Into Night is a companion piece to Kaili Blues (2015),  which is quite acclaimed as well. 
  - > I was lucky to have a local theatre also show Long Days Journey into Night 

Man would I love to live where they play movies like that in the theater. I wonder what it costs to open and run a small indie theater that just runs old or lesser known films all the time, I'd probably have Wong Kar-Wai month once a year...not sure it'd be popular but my azz would be in a seat for sure.

Also that Apple scene was intense, my man was dialed in lol
2. I’ve been meaning to make time to rewatch it. I watched it a few months ago at night and I was quite tired so I was half asleep for a section in the middle. Despite this I actually found it to be one of those films that being sleepy added to the experience given the dreamlike nature of the film. It put me in a sort of trance. Maybe it’s just me, but other there’s dreamlike films that I feel the same way about and have come to kind of embrace. But I don’t remember much about the film in detail except for the final section so I’ve been feeling like I owe it a rewatch
  - A lot is lost in translation for Western audiences. It's not just a dream or an illusion in the typical Western sense, but something deeply rooted in Buddhist religion and philosophy as a whole: the concept of samsara, reincarnation, attachment, the Heart Sutra, emptiness, enlightened beings, and so on. These ideas aren't part of the collective cultural memory of most Western societies, so many of the layers are inevitably lost.

The same applies to Chinese history. The first story represents the first part of the 20th century, with the legacy of the Opium Wars and the decline of the Qing dynasty leading toward the Republic; the second is connected to the Republican era; the third to the Mao era; the fourth to the Reform and Opening Up period, from 1978 toward the end of the century; and the last one takes us to the end of the 20th century in a view toward the present day.

And if you think about it, each of these historical periods also corresponds to different eras of cinema, with their own classical references, while the entire structure is simultaneously built around Buddhist philosophy — all of this while creating an analogy between cinema itself as a space for collective dreams and the role of art in an increasingly technological society. I honestly have no words. 

And on top of all that, there's the sheer mastery of the film's technical language.
  - Me falling asleep to David lynch only to get jumpscared by dumpster man
3. I saw it twice last year at my local film festival. I was floored by it, definitely my favourite of last year. 

Thats so interesting what you’ve written about each of the segments alluding to various chapters in China’s political history. Im not so familiar with that history so will absolutely be thinking of this when I watch it again. 

I’ve read also that each story represents a particular sense (components of the Buddhist view of mind) 
The first story is sight (silent film), the second is sound (about â violinist), the third is taste (the spirit of bitterness), the fourth is smell (waking and sleeping in a bed of oranges) and the fifth is touch. 
Others have probably written about that better than I have. 

I noticed on my most recent viewing that the Monster is the film itself, each story representing a sense, â part of its mind, and the total film as it’s screened is it’s Resurrection. 

Also that each chapter is a sort of palindrome, and the film itself is bookended by mirrored reflections. 

The opening story begins with a cinema screen burning open, inviting us into the dream like a portal. We meet the Fantasmer as a Monster. 

The second story begins by crashing through a window into a train-car bed, and introduces the idea of “stepping through the mirror.” 
The final scene of this story crashes through the very same train-car window. There’s also several scenes shot backwards and played in reverse, some subtle and some not so subtle. 

The third story begins with the mongrel (aka 
mixed breed
 dog, just like the monster/fantasmer) coming up the path to the Temple. 
The final scene is of the dog walking down that same path. 

The fourth story begins with the fantasmer sleeping on a truck full of oranges. 
The final scene is of him sleeping/dead on a truck full of oranges. 

The fifth story begins with our characters meeting at the dock. It climbs all the way up to the Sunrise Bar before winding all the way back down, concluding at the very same dock during sunrise. 

The film as a whole then concludes with the dreamer becoming the very monster we meet in the opening chapter. We then watch a cinema screen as it melts away instead of burns. 
 

I love how many ways of experiencing and understanding this film there are. Truly a work of poetry. 
 
  - Yes, the five senses are related to the Heart Sutra. The concepts you mentioned are also interesting - I'm still processing everything lol. The dream/illusion is obviously the main topic of the movie, no matter from what perspective you approach it. One of the things that makes this movie truly a masterpiece, in my opinion, is that, besides its compelling cinematic language, it has several layers and multiple meanings that allow you to enjoy it regardless of whether you grasp one, two, or more of them, or of the interpretations you give them.

4. We were fortunate to have a two week run of this earlier this year at a local indie cinema. I ended up watching it twice during that time.  

While I recognized the eras of cinema that were being referenced, the parallels with Chinese history were largely lost on me absent the context. Regardless, it remained engrossing, but you’ve got to meet the film on the director’s terms. That’s why I was *compelled* to see it in the theatre twice. This is a film that deserves one’s full attention and focus (and rewards you for it).

I understand the struggle to speak about it. It very much feels like describing a dream. To merely recount what happened is to reduce the cumulative effect it has between sight, sound and the perception of time. But most importantly what it meant to me, filtered through my own lens of memories and experiences. Which seems appropriate given some of the events in the film. 
  - I'd have loved to have watched it in a cinema.

## 3. Orson Welles’ Macbeth (1948)

**Score:** 20
**Body:** I try to avoid the word “underrated” in the film context. What does it really mean? So I won’t start today, but Welles’ least-regarded of his Shakespearean adaptations is one of the great renderings of the Bard on film.

It is at the same time theatrical and intensely cinematic. The second-hand sets and costumes feel more at home on a stage. The long takes (one exceeds 15 minutes) lend that real-time sense of the theatre too.

But the camera is what makes this adaptation special. Bogdanovich relates that Welles called it a “charcoal sketch” of the Scottish Play. It’s an apt compliment even if this isn’t what Welles meant.

Light flickers off damp cavern walls. Gloom and murk are watchwords of the day. The famous “tomorrow and tomorrow” speech is a headless voiceover whispered while on screen a still shot of smoke curls and brews. When Macbeth himself is on screen, it’s almost always an ironic low shot. Shadows constantly spill across his face. A man wracked by guilt and shame and fear.

The costumes build on this atmosphere. Highlighted by Macbeth’s infamously clunky crowns, Welles plays the antihero as a dunce. The clownish foreboding score backs it up.  There’s a hint of comedy in Welles’s depiction of the titular figure. I must admit (this is probably my 4th viewing) that this eluded me at first but I think the film reveals the most in this light.

The priest (a Welles invention, I think) adds a mystical, spiritual quality complementing and as a foil to the 3 witches.  Is this fate or are greater forces manipulating these events? And which side is winning? The rustic staves carried by the soldiers, the crosses atop the helms of MacDuff’s army, feel like religious iconography. Crowd and battle scenes surely owe a debt to Eisenstein.

Welles, to me, translates these works to screen better than anyone (with tremendous respect to Olivier and in particular his Richard III) because they are not filmed plays. They are real artistic interpretations. It’s hard to recall a single conventional shot in the whole film. Each angle and shadow adds a little more to the themes at play here. Power and its follies, drenched in shadows and fog.

Welles said he never liked acting as much as directing (per Bogdanovich again), but he’s at his best on that side of the camera in his Shakespeare adaptations. It’s like watching a master soloist on the instrument. No note is missed and there’s intent behind each syllable.  As good as his performance is (Banquo’s ghost scene is a treat), the Lady Macbeth performance matches it.

Maybe we’ll see a day where this is mentioned among Welles best.

## 4. I think "Alexander: The Ultimate Cut" is very similar to "The Odyssey (2026)" in terms of quality. This is not an insult to The Odyssey, but more of a reappraisal of Alexander.

**Score:** 17
**Body:** I think both films are very good, but ultimately flawed. They are certainly enjoyable watches, and made with great passion. 

I think the biggest flaws of both films is acting and dialogue. Both films are guilty of exposition heavy dialogue. I think the dialogue in The Odyssey was too bland, but it may have been overly theatrical in Alexander.

The overly theatrical dialogue was not helped by some very over the top performances at times. Though I do think these performances get too much hate. They all have their moments, and Val Kilmer is perfect. Colin Farrell's performance was surprisingly moving at times. Certain scenes could have been done better, but he was quite touching overall. I personally felt slightly more invested in Farrell's Alexander than Damon's Odysseus. 

I think the performances in the odyssey ranged from great to boring to overacting. I don't think Damon was bad actually, but Nolan has a habit of leaving his protagonists slightly difficult to reach. Stone may have gone too far in the opposite direction, but I did feel there were higher stakes. I think Anne Hathaway did overact in her scenes with Tom Holland. Holland in turn was like wood in those scenes. But they were alright overall, if not exceptional. I think John Leguizamo, Samantha Morton, and Robert Pattinson were all great. 

Ultimately these flaws are easily overlooked due to the scale and technical beauty of the films. Alexander has huge battles, and captivating sets. The charging scene in India was so perfect. Each location on Alexander's journey is beautifully done and unique. Films are rarely at this scale, so it's just enjoyable to watch. 

The odyssey is equally as beautiful. Nolan managed to keep every part of the journey captivating. The scenes at Troy were particularly engaging. Nolan's insistence on practical effects paid off. Like Alexander, it's just a spectacle we rarely see. 

The pacing is also great. I never felt bored or distracted during the odyssey, it commanded my focus completely. Similarly Alexander's Ultimate Cut has perfected it's pacing. The film famously had four versions. The original theatrical cut was rushed and sloppy. The second cut too much. The third cut, the so-called "final cut" was too bloated. But the ultimate cut, the true final cut, was perfect. It managed to tell Alexander's story in a full and satisfying way, without being a long drag. Alexander was an extremely ambitious project, but I do think Stone eventually achieved his vision with the ultimate cut.

These are both excellent films made by some of the finest directors around. I believe anyone who's a fan of epics will find some joy from these films.

## 5. What did you think of the color grading in the Odyssey?

**Score:** 9
**Body:** When the trailer for this movie dropped, so much of the discourse centered around Nolan’s apparent decision to take a vibrant, colorful story and make it drab and lifeless with his a desaturated color palette. 

After watching the movie twice, I decided that the color grading was fairly tasteful. Some movies (Marvel being the main culprit) seem to think that just adding a gray scale filter to cinematography will somehow automatically make it more serious. However, the de saturated color grading in the odyssey felt like it fit with the subjective state of the characters. In desecrating zeus’s law, they have taken warmth and joy out of a once vibrant civilization. 

Furthermore, I feel like there was a fair amount of variety to the color palette, actually. Lots of deep resonant blues that gave off an eerie sense of beauty. The dark scenes were gorgeous - especially the sequence in Hades dominated by charcoal. The frequent use of firelight as the main source of lighting added some multi dimensionality as well. While this was a fairly desaturated movie, it wasn’t just an endless slog of drab gray. 

What did you think about Nolan’s color choices here? Should he have gone with a more vibrant color palette, or did he make the right choice?
